_meta.source: Ephrem the Syrian + Cyril of Alexandria + 1 Enoch references — seed corpus shipped with γ.4 (2026-05-11). γ.4.1.A (2026-05-12) added Cyril on John 1-4 (30 entries). γ.4.1.B (2026-05-12) added Cyril on John 5-7 (27 entries: Bethesda discourse + Bread of Life + Tabernacles/Living Water). All Cyril material sourced from NPNF Series 2 vol. 14 (Pusey/Randell translation, Oxford 1874-1885).
_meta.scope: Curated interpretive summaries verse-keyed to passages where the Ethiopian Tewahedo tradition carries a distinctive reading. The Syriac (Ephrem) and non-Chalcedonian Alexandrian (Cyril) fathers are the patristic anchors shared by the Oriental Orthodox communion; Ethiopia is one of its five canonical jurisdictions. 1 Enoch is included specifically because Tewahedo is the only major communion to canonize it; the references draw on R.H. Charles' PD 1912 translation. Each entry is a paraphrased summary, not a verbatim quote. γ.4 shipped 12 seed entries; γ.4.1.A (2026-05-12) added 30 Cyril-on-John entries covering John 1-4 (Logos prologue + John the Baptist + Cana + Temple cleansing + Nicodemus + Samaritan woman); γ.4.1.B (2026-05-12) added 27 entries covering John 5-7 (Bethesda + discourse on the Son + Bread of Life + Tabernacles + Living Water/Spirit). Cyril is now the heaviest single voice in the corpus (62 of 69 total entries). Future γ.4.1.C-D will extend to John 11-21 (noting Cyril's Books VII-VIII on Jn 8-10 are LOST in manuscript tradition); γ.4.2-6 will cover Ephrem on Genesis + Cyril on Luke + 1 Enoch + Ephrem's Hymns on Paradise + Cyril's Letters.
_meta.public_domain_basis: Ephrem the Syrian d. 373 AD (NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. Gwynn / Schaff, 1898). Cyril of Alexandria d. 444 AD (NPNF Series 2, vols. 7 + 14, trans. P.E. Pusey + Thomas Randell, Oxford: James Parker, 1874-1885 — both translators died well before 1929: Pusey d. 1880, Randell d. 1899). R.H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon, 1912 — PD). All translations cited are out of copyright in every jurisdiction.

entries.work: Commentary on Genesis
entries.summary: Ephrem reads 'In the beginning' as denoting the absolute commencement of created time, not a moment within a prior temporal sequence. The Word through whom God creates is not added to creation but is its enabling cause; thus the verse is read Christologically without dissolving the Father-Son distinction. Ethiopian Tewahedo commentary follows Ephrem on this point against any reading that would make the Son a creature.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Prologue. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.

entries.work: Hymns on Paradise
entries.summary: On 'Let there be light', Ephrem distinguishes the first-day light from the fourth-day luminaries: the primordial light is the radiance of God's own glory illuminating creation before its instruments (sun, moon, stars) are fashioned. The Ethiopian Andəmta homily extends this by identifying the seven days as a typological prefigurement of the seven ages of salvation history culminating in Christ.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on Paradise I.4-7. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.work: Thesaurus on the Holy and Consubstantial Trinity
entries.summary: Cyril reads the plural 'Let us make' as the Trinity in council, the Father addressing the Son and the Holy Spirit — not a royal plural and not (against the Jewish reading) the angels, since the image is divine and angels are not creators. The image is located primarily in the rational soul. This Trinitarian construction is held without modification by Tewahedo dogmatics; the Miaphysite formula of Cyril ('one nature of the incarnate Word') governs the subsequent reading of human nature in Christ.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Thesaurus, Assertion XVII. NPNF Series 2, vol. 7. PD.

entries.work: Commentary on Genesis
entries.summary: On 'God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life', Ephrem reads the breath (nefesh / nešmā) not as a separable substance but as the divine in-spiration that gives Adam his unique standing among creatures. The Ethiopian Andəmta commentary on this verse stresses that the breath is what makes the human a fitting addressee for revelation — not merely a living animal but a hearer of the Word.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis II.2. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.

entries.work: Commentary on Genesis
entries.summary: Ephrem's reading of the serpent emphasizes deception by speech rather than ontological evil: the serpent is a creature whose form Satan borrows for the purpose of the temptation. Tewahedo tradition, drawing on the Synaxarium accounts of the Watchers (cf. 1 Enoch 6-11), connects this fallen-angel-acting-through-a-beast pattern to the wider angelology of the Ethiopian canon.
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis II.15. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. (Watchers parallel: R.H. Charles, Book of Enoch, 1912, ch. 6-11.)

entries.work: Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 6-11)
entries.summary: Where the Hebrew Bible's 'sons of God' (b'nei ha'elohim) saw the daughters of men, the Ethiopian Tewahedo tradition reads through 1 Enoch's expansion: the Watchers, two hundred angels under Semjâzâ, descend on Mount Hermon and bind themselves by oath to take human wives. The corruption is not human alone but angelic-human, requiring the Flood as a cosmic — not merely punitive — purgation. The Tewahedo canon is the only Christian canon to receive 1 Enoch as Scripture, making this reading load-bearing for its theology of evil.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 6:1-8, trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon, 1912). PD. The Ethiopic Mäṣḥafä Hēnok preserves the only complete text.

entries.work: Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 6-11)
entries.summary: The Nephilim ('giants') of Genesis 6:4 are, in 1 Enoch's reading received by Tewahedo, the half-angelic offspring of the Watchers' union with human women. They are not figures of valor but of disorder; their consumption of all that humans could produce and their turning on humanity is the proximate cause of the Flood. Jude 1:14-15's direct quotation of 1 Enoch confirms the New Testament's acquaintance with this tradition.
entries.attribution: 1 Enoch 7:1-6 + 8:1-3, trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1912). PD. Cf. Jude 1:14-15 quoting 1 Enoch 1:9 verbatim.

entries.work: Commentary on the Psalms
entries.summary: Ephrem opens his Psalter commentary with the threefold negation — walks not / stands not / sits not — as a progression of deepening complicity in evil: the walk is occasional, the standing is habitual, the sitting is settled. The Ethiopian Andəmta tradition develops this into a homiletic device for the daily examen, paired with the threefold ascent of the just (meditation by day / by night / yielding fruit in season).
entries.attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, on Psalm 1. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13 (Gwynn). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Psalms
entries.summary: Cyril reads 'The Lord is my shepherd' Christologically: the shepherd of Psalm 23 is the same as the Good Shepherd of John 10, the same as the Lamb of Revelation. The 'I shall not want' is a confession of complete dependence on the Incarnate Word who is at once Lamb and Shepherd. Tewahedo liturgy preserves this Christological reading prominently in the burial office.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, on Psalm 22/23 (LXX numbering). NPNF Series 2, vol. 7. PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: On the Logos prologue, Cyril resists any temporal reading of 'in the beginning was the Word': the Word is co-eternal with the Father, not produced as the first effect of the Father's will. Cyril's Miaphysite formula — 'one nature of the incarnate Word' — anchors the Tewahedo christological tradition; the Ethiopian Liturgy of St Cyril ('Anaphora of Cyril of Alexandria') is one of the principal eucharistic prayers of the Ethiopian Church to this day.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.1 (NPNF S2 V14, Pusey/Randell trans., Oxford 1874-1885). PD. Tewahedo liturgical witness: Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase, Anaphora of Cyril.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'The Word became flesh' is, for Cyril, the dogmatic foundation of the Miaphysite confession received by Tewahedo: one incarnate nature of the Word, indivisibly united from two natures (divine and human) without confusion. Against the Nestorian reading that finds two persons or two natures-after-union, Cyril insists the union is hypostatic and indivisible. The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors Cyril on the 3rd of Hamlē for this defense.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.14 (NPNF S2 V14, Pusey/Randell trans., Oxford 1874-1885) + Second Letter to Nestorius. PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: On the blood and water from Christ's pierced side, Cyril reads sacramentally: the water signifies baptism, the blood signifies the eucharist, both flowing from the wound that is the source of the Church's life. The Tewahedo liturgical tradition preserves this dual symbolism with particular emphasis in the Anaphora of Our Lord Jesus Christ; the wound is the Church's font and table.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.19. NPNF Series 2, vol. 14. PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'All things were made through Him' Cyril takes as a comprehensive denial of any creaturely status in the Son: the Word is not among things made, but is Himself the Maker. Cyril notes the deliberate Johannine choice of 'di' autou' (through Him) rather than 'hyp' autou' (by Him): the preposition does not subordinate the Son to the Father (as Arians read) but expresses the eternal Trinitarian order, the Father acting through the Son as His co-eternal Word. The Tewahedo Anaphora of the Apostles preserves this verse's anti-Arian cadence in its prayer of consecration: 'through whom all things were made'.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.3 (NPNF S2 V14). PD (Pusey/Randell trans., Oxford 1874-1885).

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'In Him was life, and the life was the light of men' Cyril reads as the Son's eternal possession of life — not life received, but life owned. The Word is the source of life for every creature that lives, and the life He bestows is also light: the rational illumination that distinguishes humanity. Cyril builds toward his pneumatological argument: this life-and-light shared by the Word with humanity is the prefiguring of the Spirit's later indwelling. The Tewahedo baptismal liturgy preserves this connection: candidates are addressed as those returning to the Light-of-the-Word that was theirs in creation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.4 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'The light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not' Cyril reads as the post-lapsarian condition of humanity: the Word's light continues to shine (creation has not extinguished it) but the darkness of human sin and demonic deception fails to receive it. The Greek 'katelaben' carries the double sense of 'comprehend' and 'overcome' — Cyril preserves both: the darkness neither understands the Light nor masters it. The verse becomes for Cyril the Christological hinge: the Word continues to shine in every conscience even before the Incarnation, and continues afterward despite humanity's refusal.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.5 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'The true Light, which lighteth every man, was coming into the world' Cyril reads against the Manichaean and gnostic readings of his day: the Word's illumination is universal, not restricted to a spiritual elite. Every rational creature receives some measure of the Word's light — this is what makes humanity capable of recognizing Christ when He comes in the flesh. Cyril notes the imperfect tense 'was coming' (erchomenon) as anticipating the Incarnation: the eternal illumination has always been preparing humanity for the historical advent of the Word made flesh.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.9 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'He came unto His own, and His own received Him not' Cyril reads with characteristic precision: 'His own' (ta idia) refers in the first sense to the Jewish people whom He had elected as His covenant possession, but in the broader sense to all humanity whom He had created. The double rejection (covenantal + creational) frames the Incarnation as the Maker's return to a world that has forgotten Him. For Cyril this is no Marcionite cancellation of Israel but the painful pathos of God's faithfulness meeting human refusal — the verse becomes the textual root of medieval Tewahedo homiletic readings of the prophetic ministry.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.11 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'As many as received Him, to them He gave the right (exousia) to become children of God' Cyril reads as the gift of adoptive sonship through participation in the natural Sonship of the Word. The 'exousia' is not merely permission but operative power — divine grace that effects what it confers. Cyril here begins his exposition of theosis: humans become 'children' (tekna, lower than 'huios') not by nature but by gift, through the Spirit's adoption that conforms them to Christ's image. This adoptive doctrine is foundational for the Tewahedo understanding of baptism as the moment of theosis-by-participation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.12 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God' Cyril reads as the threefold negation of every natural-genealogical claim to divine sonship: Jewish ancestry (blood), human reproductive desire (will of flesh), patriarchal authority (will of man) all fail to constitute the new birth. Only the Spirit's begetting through baptism produces children of God. Cyril notes that this verse is the conceptual seed of the later baptismal regeneration doctrine — the new birth is Trinitarian in structure (the Father's gift, the Son's mediation, the Spirit's effecting) and ecclesial in setting (administered in the Church's baptismal economy).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.13 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'No man hath seen God at any time; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He hath declared Him' is for Cyril the dogmatic statement of the Son's unique revelatory office. 'In the bosom of the Father' (eis ton kolpon tou Patros) Cyril reads not spatially but as expressing intimate co-substantiality and eternal mutual indwelling. The Son's revelation is not derivative testimony but the Father's self-disclosure in His own Word. Against Eunomian rationalism (which claimed direct knowledge of the divine essence), Cyril here grounds Christian epistemology in the Son's mediation: we know the Father only through the Son who eternally knows Him.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk I.18 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: On John the Baptist's self-identification as 'the voice of one crying in the wilderness' (citing Isa 40:3), Cyril develops the patristic distinction between Voice (phone) and Word (logos): the Baptist is the audible preparation for the eternal Word's manifestation. The Voice is heard, then ceases; the Word abides forever. The 'wilderness' Cyril reads typologically: not merely the Judean desert but the spiritual barrenness of pre-Incarnational humanity awaiting the Word's coming. The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors the Baptist as the 'lamp of Christ' on the 30th of Hidar, preserving this Voice-Word distinction in its liturgical hymnody.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.23 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' Cyril reads as the typological climax of the entire Hebrew sacrificial economy: the Paschal lamb of Exodus, the lambs of the daily burnt offering, the Isaianic lamb led to the slaughter — all converge in the Baptist's pointing finger. The 'taketh away' (airon) Cyril stresses as present-tense ongoing action: the Lamb's atoning work is not a single historical moment but the perpetual offering perpetually applied through the Church's eucharistic representation. This sacrificial-eucharistic reading is foundational to the Tewahedo Anaphora's offertory prayers.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.29 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending and remaining (menon) on Him' Cyril reads with characteristic pneumatological depth: the Spirit's *remaining* (not just descending) distinguishes Christ from all the prophets, on whom the Spirit had come and departed. The Spirit's permanent indwelling of the incarnate Word is the source of every subsequent gift of the Spirit to humanity — what Christ possesses by nature, He communicates to the baptized by participation. Cyril here grounds his entire pneumatology in the Jordan event: the Holy Spirit's mission to the Church flows from His abiding upon the Son.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.33 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man' Cyril reads as the Christological fulfillment of Jacob's ladder vision (Gen 28:12): the incarnate Christ IS the ladder uniting heaven and earth in His own Person. The angels' bidirectional movement signifies the restored communication between divinity and creation through the Word made flesh. Cyril notes that this is the first explicit messianic self-identification in John's Gospel ('Son of man') and that it grounds the entire subsequent series of theophanic 'I am' sayings.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.51 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Cyril carefully defends Christ's address to His mother at Cana ('Woman, what have I to do with thee?') against any reading that would imply disrespect. 'Woman' (gynai) is for Cyril a formal address of honor, not familiarity-refused; the question is rhetorical, situating the miracle within His Father's appointed timing rather than maternal pressure. Mary's authority remains intact (she immediately directs the servants to obey Christ) — the verse establishes the principle that Christ's miracles proceed from the Father's will, not human request, even when that human is His own mother. Tewahedo Marian veneration preserves this delicate balance.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.4 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Fill the waterpots with water' Cyril reads as the typological pivot of the entire Cana sign: Christ deliberately requires human cooperation (the servants' labor of filling) before the divine transformation. The six stone waterpots — used for Jewish purification rites — Cyril reads as the six days of creation (the imperfect order awaiting completion), or as the Old Covenant's purification economy awaiting Christ's New Covenant fulfillment. The water-to-wine transformation prefigures the eucharistic transformation: the elements remain (water/bread), but their inner reality is changed by Christ's word.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.7 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: On 'This beginning of miracles did Jesus' Cyril notes the programmatic placement: a wedding-feast miracle inaugurates the public ministry, signaling that Christ's mission is nuptial in character — He has come to wed humanity to divinity in His own flesh. 'Manifested forth His glory' (ephanerōsen tēn doxan autou) Cyril reads as the proleptic revelation of the cross's glory: the Cana glory and the Calvary glory are one glory, the glory of the eternal Word visible in His incarnate works. The disciples' belief that follows is the first-fruits of the entire Church's faith.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.11 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up' is for Cyril a Christological saying of central importance: the temple in question is not Herod's structure but Christ's body, and the active agent of the Resurrection is the Son Himself ('I will raise it up' — egerō auton). Against subordinationist readings that would make the Resurrection a passive event done TO Christ by the Father, Cyril insists on the Son's active agency: the Word raises His own assumed humanity through the divine power that is His own by nature. This is the dogmatic root of the Tewahedo Easter Anaphora's doxology of the Risen Christ as agent of His own resurrection.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.19 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: John's interpretive aside — 'He spake of the temple of His body' — provides Cyril his exegetical warrant for body-as-temple typology that runs throughout his John commentary. The Old Covenant temple (with its court of Gentiles, holy place, holy of holies) prefigures the structure of the incarnate Christ: His flesh is the new court where Gentiles enter, His soul the new holy place, His divinity the new holy of holies indwelt by the Father. This temple-Christology extends to ecclesiology: the Church as Christ's body inherits the temple typology, with baptism replacing circumcision as the gateway and the eucharist replacing the daily sacrifice as the perpetual offering.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.21 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Except a man be born again (anōthen), he cannot see the kingdom of God' is for Cyril the doctrinal axis of the entire Nicodemus pericope. The Greek 'anōthen' carries the double sense of 'again' (temporal) and 'from above' (spatial); Cyril preserves both: the new birth is at once a second temporal beginning AND a heavenly-origined event, not produced from human sources. This rebirth is necessary not as supplement to natural birth but as substitute for it on the order of grace: what natural birth gives (mortality, sin-inheritance, alienation from God) the rebirth replaces (incorruption, adoption, communion). The verse is the locus classicus for the Tewahedo doctrine of baptism as ontological renovation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.3 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit' Cyril reads as the dominical institution of baptism: the two elements (water and Spirit) are inseparable, not sequential. Against the Messalians and other spiritualizing groups who would dispense with water and rely on a purely interior Spirit-experience, Cyril insists that the Spirit binds Himself to the water-sign in the Church's sacramental administration. The water is not merely symbolic accompaniment but the divinely-chosen visible vehicle of the Spirit's invisible regenerating act. This sacramental realism is the textual ground of the entire Tewahedo baptismal theology.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.5 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit' Cyril reads as Johannine confirmation of the doctrine of original sin: flesh begets only flesh, and the natural process of generation cannot transmit anything beyond the conditions of fallen creaturehood. Only the Spirit's begetting communicates spiritual life. Cyril is careful here to distinguish his reading from Manichaean dualism: 'flesh' is not evil per se but is wounded and unable to ascend to spiritual life without supernatural elevation. The Spirit's birth does not destroy the flesh but heals and elevates it — preparing for the bodily resurrection.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.6 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: On 'The wind bloweth where it listeth' Cyril makes the most of the Greek pneuma's double sense (wind / spirit): the meteorological observation grounds the pneumatological doctrine. The Spirit's working in regeneration is sovereign (chooses its own subjects), audible-in-effects (the voice is heard), but invisible-in-cause (we cannot trace its origin or destination). Against Pelagian readings that would make human will the operative cause of regeneration, Cyril insists the Spirit's freedom is primary: regeneration is sovereign gift, even where it is mediated through baptism's prescribed channels. The Spirit who fills the prescribed channels is not bound by them.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.8 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'No man hath ascended up to heaven, but He that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven' is a verse Cyril uses to defend the *communicatio idiomatum* — the communication of attributes between Christ's divine and human natures in His one Person. The Son of man is 'in heaven' even while speaking to Nicodemus on earth: the divine attribute (omnipresence) is predicated of the human Person (Son of man) by virtue of the hypostatic union. Against Nestorian dilution (which would assign heavenly attributes only to the Logos-Person and earthly attributes only to the human-Person), Cyril here grounds the Miaphysite confession in Christ's own Johannine self-witness.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.13 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Christ's typological self-reference — 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up' — Cyril develops with characteristic typological care. The bronze serpent was a likeness of the agent of death (the serpent) elevated as the means of healing; Christ on the cross is the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom 8:3) elevated as the means of salvation. The 'must' (dei) Cyril reads as expressing not external necessity (the schemes of His enemies) but the Father's eternal redemptive will to which the Son freely conforms. The Tewahedo Holy Week liturgy preserves this typological reading prominently.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.14 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: On the most-cited verse in the Gospel — 'For God so loved the world, that He gave His only-begotten Son' — Cyril builds the Athanasian-Cappadocian Trinitarian framework: the Father's love for the world is so radical that He gives not merely a creature or a prophet but His own consubstantial Son. The 'gave' (edōken) refers both to the Incarnation (the eternal Son's mission into flesh) and to the cross (the giving up to death) — the two are one redemptive movement. 'Only-begotten' (monogenēs) excludes any creaturely sonship: the Son's relation to the Father is unique, eternal, and inseparable. Cyril notes that 'the world' (kosmos) here means the whole of humanity, not the elect-narrowly — universal scope of love, particular efficacy of salvation through faith.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.16 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him' — for Cyril this Baptist's final discourse is also a Christological confession: the Son is the criterion of judgment. 'Hath' (echei, present tense) Cyril stresses: eternal life is not merely future promise but present possession of the believer through union with Christ. 'Abideth' (menei) for the wrath similarly denotes present condition, not future sentence: unbelief is itself the judgment, since refusing the Son cuts off from the only source of life. Cyril here grounds the realized-eschatology dimension of Johannine theology against any purely futurist readings.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.36 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Christ's promise to the Samaritan woman — 'Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life' — Cyril reads pneumatologically: the water is the Holy Spirit Himself, given through Christ as His own gift to those who receive Him. The water's spring inside the believer (pēgē hydatos hallomenou) figures the Spirit's permanent indwelling, distinguished from the Old Covenant prophetic intermittent inspiration. 'Springing up' (hallomenou) carries the sense of leaping, dynamic ascent — the Spirit's indwelling is not static container but living source of theosis.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.14 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'The hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth' Cyril reads as the abrogation of the geographic-cultic restriction (Jerusalem temple / Mt. Gerizim) in favor of pneumatic-Christological worship. 'In spirit' is for Cyril 'in the Holy Spirit' (the worshipper's pneumatic transformation), and 'in truth' is 'in the Truth that is Christ' (Jn 14:6). True worship after the Incarnation is therefore Trinitarian: to the Father, in the Spirit, through the Truth-Son. This passage grounds the Tewahedo liturgical doctrine that the Anaphora's prayer is itself the Spirit's praying through the Church to the Father, mediated by the Christological elements.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.23 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'God is a Spirit' (pneuma ho theos) — Cyril reads this as ontological statement (the divine nature is spiritual, not material) and as missiological imperative (those who would worship a spiritual God must be spiritually transformed). Against the Anthropomorphites who attributed bodily form to God, Cyril insists the verse settles the question: God has no parts, no extension, no spatial location. Yet against any Hellenizing collapse of God into pure abstraction, Cyril preserves the personal-relational character: the Spirit-God is the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit — three Persons in one spiritual essence. Worship 'in spirit and in truth' is therefore the only worship corresponding to God's actual mode of being.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.24 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'My meat is to do the will of Him that sent me, and to finish His work' Cyril reads as Christ's self-disclosure of the perfect harmony between His human will and the Father's eternal will. Against the Apollinarian denial of Christ's human soul (or against any reading that would make Christ's will merely divine), Cyril here recognizes that Christ has a genuinely human will, but it is so perfectly conformed to the Father's will that 'doing the Father's will' becomes His characteristic sustenance — what physical food is to bodily life, the doing of the divine will is to Christ's incarnate human life. This is the seed of the dyothelite-anticipation that becomes explicit in later Greek theology, though Cyril himself does not yet use those terms.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.34 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: The Samaritans' climactic confession — 'This is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world' (ho sōtēr tou kosmou) — Cyril emphasizes as the proleptic Gentile recognition of Christ's universal salvific scope. The Samaritans, themselves marginal to Jewish covenant identity, become the prototype for the Gentile inclusion that will mark the post-Pentecost Church. 'Saviour of the world' is for Cyril a title both universal (Christ saves the world, not merely a portion) and particular (each person is saved as individual within that universal scope). The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors Photine (the traditional name of the Samaritan woman) on the 26th of Hidar — her witness to her village becomes the first apostolic missionary act recorded in John.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.42 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: Christ's command to the paralytic — 'Rise, take up thy bed, and walk' — Cyril reads as the threefold pattern of every healing the Word performs in the soul: resurrection from spiritual death (rise), taking up the burden of one's former weakness as instrument rather than master (take up thy bed), and active progress in the new life (walk). The thirty-eight years of paralysis Cyril typologically links with the thirty-eight years of Israel's wilderness wandering (Deut 2:14) — both the individual and the people are healed by direct sovereign address, not by mediating ceremony or stirred-pool waiting. The Sabbath setting prepares Cyril's larger argument: Christ exercises the Father's authority over the Sabbath because He is consubstantial with the Father.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.8 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' (heōs arti) — Cyril reads as one of the most decisive anti-Arian sayings in the Gospel. The Sabbath rest of Gen 2:2 did not mean God ceased operating (providence is unbroken); Christ here claims the same uninterrupted operative power that belongs to the Father. The 'and I' (kagō) refuses any subordination: the Son's working is co-equal, co-eternal, co-extensive with the Father's. The Jews' immediate reaction (5:18: they sought to kill Him for 'making Himself equal with God') confirms they understood the claim correctly. Cyril uses this verse against the Eusebian semi-Arians of his own day who would dilute the Son's operative parity with the Father.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.17 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: The Jews' interpretation — that Christ was 'making Himself equal with God' (ison heauton poiōn tō Theō) — Cyril takes as inspired witness, not hostile misreading. Even Christ's opponents recognized that calling God 'my Father' (idion Patera) in this manner was a claim to consubstantial equality, not adoptive sonship. Cyril notes the Greek 'idion' (own/proper) carries the sense of natural-not-merely-adoptive: the Son's relation to the Father differs in kind, not just degree, from any creature's. This verse is one of Cyril's strongest scriptural anchors against Arian and Eunomian readings — even the unbelieving witnesses confirm the orthodox reading.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.18 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He seeth the Father do' Cyril reads with extreme care against Arian misreading. The 'can do nothing of Himself' is NOT a statement of weakness or subordination but of perfect Trinitarian harmony: the Son's operations are inseparable from the Father's because of their consubstantial unity. The 'seeing' is not perceptual observation (as if the Son had to watch what the Father did) but eternal mutual indwelling of co-equal Persons. 'What things soever He doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise' (homoiōs) Cyril stresses: not subordinately, not differently, but identically — every divine work belongs to all three Persons indivisibly.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.19 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'As the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them; even so the Son quickeneth whom He will' — Cyril takes the absolute power of the eschatological resurrection as the supreme proof of consubstantiality. To raise the dead is a work exclusively divine; for the Son to share this power without limit means He shares the divine nature. 'Whom He will' (hous thelei) Cyril emphasizes: not a delegated authority to be exercised within constraints, but sovereign personal choice — the same will that the Father exercises. The verse also establishes the personalist character of resurrection: Christ raises individuals by His sovereign decision, not as automatic effect of cosmic process.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.21 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'The Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son' Cyril reads as the eschatological consummation of the Father-Son economy: the Father's universal judgment is exercised through the incarnate Son, who because of His shared human nature is uniquely fit to judge humanity. The 'committed' (dedōken) Cyril carefully distinguishes from any subordinationist reading: this is not a delegation of authority the Father lacks the will to exercise directly, but the manifestation of the eternal Trinitarian order — every operation 'from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit' (Cyril's standard formula). This verse grounds Cyril's later argument (in the Twelve Anathemas) that the man-God Christ, not a separate human judge, presides at the Last Day.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.22 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'He that heareth my word, and believeth on Him that sent me, HATH everlasting life' Cyril reads as one of the strongest realized-eschatology pins in the Gospel: eternal life is not merely promised for the future but present possession of the believer through faith. 'Is passed from death unto life' (metabebēken — perfect tense, completed action with continuing result) confirms the present reality: the believer has ALREADY transitioned from the death-realm to the life-realm. This is not denial of future bodily resurrection (which Cyril affirms strongly) but recognition that the spiritual-ontological transition has already occurred for those united to Christ by faith. The verse grounds Cyril's sacramental realism: baptism enacts what faith receives.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.24 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'As the Father hath life in Himself, so hath He given to the Son to have life in Himself' is for Cyril a critical text for the Son's natural-not-derived divinity. The 'given' (edōken) is not temporal grant (as if the Son did not always possess what He now has) but eternal communication of essence — the Father eternally communicates to the Son the same divine life He has from Himself. To 'have life in Himself' (echein zōēn en heautō) is the divine attribute par excellence: not life received from elsewhere, but life as one's own essence. The Father has it without source; the Son has it from the Father, yet equally and eternally. This is Cyril's most precise statement of the Cappadocian-Athanasian doctrine of eternal generation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.26 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me' Cyril takes as the dominical hermeneutical principle: the Hebrew Scriptures are properly read only when read Christologically. Against Marcion's rejection of the Old Testament and against the Jewish rejection of its messianic-Christological reading, Cyril positions the verse as Christ's own self-witness: He IS the proper subject of the Scriptures. 'Ye think' (dokeite) is gentle correction: searching the Scriptures for eternal life apart from recognizing Christ in them is futile — the life they testify to is the life He brings. This verse grounds the entire Alexandrian typological hermeneutic.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.39 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me' Cyril reads as Christ's authoritative claim to be the proper object of every Mosaic prophecy. The verse establishes the principle that Moses and Christ stand in continuity, not discontinuity: rejection of Christ is rejection of Moses (and conversely, true reception of Moses leads to Christ). Cyril uses this verse against any Manichaean or Marcionite reading that would oppose the Testaments; he also uses it against any Jewish reading that would treat Mosaic obedience as sufficient apart from Christological reception. The Tewahedo Pentateuch readings in the Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase preserve this Cyrilline unity by always pairing Torah readings with their Christological NT fulfillment.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.46 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: On the multiplication of loaves Cyril notes the deliberate eucharistic prefiguration: Christ TOOK the loaves, gave THANKS (eucharistēsas), and distributed. The four-fold pattern (take / bless / break / give) that becomes the Mass Cyril sees inaugurated here — the feeding of the five thousand is the sign that points to the institution at the Last Supper and the perpetual continuation in the Anaphora. The crowd's hunger Cyril takes typologically: humanity hungers for the bread of eternal life which only Christ can give; physical hunger is the symptom of the deeper spiritual hunger. The Tewahedo Anaphora's preparation prayers preserve this typological reading explicitly.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk III.11 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life' Cyril reads as Christ's hermeneutic for understanding the previous miracle: the loaves were sign, not substance — the substance is the eucharistic bread that gives eternal life. 'Which the Son of man shall give unto you' (dōsei — future tense) Cyril emphasizes: pointing forward to the institution of the eucharist, not to repeat-feedings of physical bread. 'For him hath God the Father sealed' Cyril reads as the Spirit's anointing that makes Christ's human nature the perpetual source of the bread of life — the seal of the Spirit on the incarnate Son is what makes the eucharistic gift possible.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk III.27 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'I am the bread of life' (egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs) — the first of Christ's great 'I AM' sayings in John — Cyril reads as both ontological self-disclosure and sacramental promise. The 'I am' echoes the divine name (Ex 3:14: ego eimi ho ōn); the 'bread of life' identifies the specific mode of Christ's gift to His Church. 'He that cometh to me shall never hunger, and he that believeth on me shall never thirst' Cyril takes as the perfect parallel between coming-to-Christ (sacramentally: through baptism into His body) and believing-on-Him (fiducially: through saving faith) — neither alone, but both together produce the perpetual satisfaction of spiritual hunger and thirst.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk III.35 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of Him that sent me' Cyril reads against any reading that would set the Son's will in opposition to the Father's. The 'not mine own' (ouch hina poiō) does not deny that the Son HAS a will (Apollinarian denial), nor does it imply imperfect alignment requiring submission. Rather, Cyril notes the Son's INCARNATE human will is now in question: as man, the Son receives the Father's will and acts upon it; as God, His will is identical with the Father's by nature. This is one of Cyril's earliest articulations of what later dyothelite theology would systematize: two wills (divine + human) in one Person, perfectly aligned.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk III.38 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him' Cyril reads as the Johannine doctrine of prevenient grace. The Father's 'drawing' (helkysē) is the operative work of grace that precedes and enables human response to Christ; without it, no one comes. Cyril is careful here against Pelagian readings: the verse strictly excludes natural human capacity to come to Christ apart from divine initiative. Yet the 'drawing' is not coercive — Cyril (following the classic patristic distinction) reads it as the Father's drawing through the Spirit's inward attraction, which the human will may still resist (against later Augustinian readings that would make it irresistible). This passage grounds the Eastern Christian doctrine of synergism: grace initiates, the will cooperates.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk III.44 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world' is for Cyril the central eucharistic-Christological text in the entire Gospel. The bread Christ gives IS His own flesh — the personal Word's true flesh, not a metaphor or symbol, but the incarnate body offered on the cross and now communicated through the eucharist. 'For the life of the world' confirms the universal scope of the offering — not for the elect alone, not for the Jews alone, but for the kosmos. Cyril uses this verse as the textual foundation for his doctrine of eucharistic realism that becomes determinative for all subsequent Greek and Oriental Orthodox theology.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk III.51 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink His blood, ye have no life in you' Cyril takes with full sacramental seriousness: this is not metaphor but ontological condition. The eucharistic eating-and-drinking is the necessary means by which the life of the incarnate Word is communicated to the believer's body and soul. Against any spiritualizing reading that would dissolve the verse into mere faith-receptive metaphor, Cyril insists the verse means what it says: the actual flesh and blood of Christ, sacramentally present, must be actually received. 'Ye have no life in you' (ouk echete zōēn en heautois) is the privative consequence of refusing the eucharistic gift. This is the locus classicus of Cyril's eucharistic theology that the Tewahedo Anaphora preserves verbatim.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk IV.53 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day' Cyril reads as the eucharistic guarantee of bodily resurrection. The flesh of Christ communicated to the believer's body becomes the seed of the resurrection body — Cyril's standard formula is that the eucharist is the 'medicine of immortality' (pharmakon athanasias, from Ignatius). The 'I will raise him up' is Christ's personal promise tied to the eucharistic reception: the body that has received the Body of Christ has within it the seed of eschatological transformation. This verse anchors Cyril's distinctive contribution to eucharistic theology: the sacrament does not merely commemorate or symbolize, it actually communicates the resurrection life.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk IV.54 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'For my flesh is meat indeed (alēthōs), and my blood is drink indeed' Cyril takes as decisive against any reading that would weaken eucharistic realism. The Greek 'alēthōs' means 'truly / really / actually' — Christ here explicitly disqualifies any metaphorical or symbolic interpretation of His preceding words. Against the gnostics of his own era and against any anticipatory spiritualizing readings, Cyril insists: TRULY flesh, REALLY blood — the eucharistic gift IS what it appears to be on the level of substance, even while remaining bread and wine to the senses. This is Cyril's clearest articulation of what later Western scholasticism would call the doctrine of real presence (without scholastic categories of substance/accidents).
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk IV.55 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'It is the Spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing' Cyril famously handles with great care against capernaitic misreadings that would take 'eating the flesh' as cannibalistic physical consumption. The 'flesh' that profiteth nothing is fleshly-mode-of-understanding, not the actual flesh of Christ (which gives life). The verse means: receiving the eucharist with merely carnal comprehension — as if Christ's body were divided physically among communicants like ordinary food — is profitless. Only Spirit-quickened reception receives the gift as it truly is. This is Cyril's careful pneumatological qualification of his strong eucharistic realism: the realism is true, but its appropriation is spiritual, not crudely physical.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk IV.63 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'My doctrine is not mine, but His that sent me' Cyril carefully defends against Arian misreading. The 'not mine' does NOT deny the Son's possession of the doctrine but identifies its source: the Son's teaching is not innovative or independent but is the eternal teaching of the Father, possessed by the Son by nature (consubstantial communication of all divine attributes including wisdom-teaching). Cyril notes the parallel to 5:30: 'I can of mine own self do nothing' — both texts speak of perfect Trinitarian harmony, not of any inferiority in the Son. The Son's teaching IS the Father's teaching because the Son IS the eternal Word who speaks the Father's mind.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk IV.16 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'If any man will do His will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God' Cyril takes as the dominical statement of moral epistemology: knowledge of divine truth is conditioned on willingness to obey. Against any purely intellectual approach to theological knowledge (which would make speculation independent of holiness), Cyril here grounds the patristic axiom: theology requires askesis. The 'will to do His will' (thelē to thelēma autou poiein) Cyril emphasizes as primary disposition; the cognitive recognition follows on it. This verse becomes the textual root of the entire Eastern Orthodox tradition that knowledge of God presupposes purification of the nous through ascetic practice.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk IV.17 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'Judge not according to the appearance (kat' opsin), but judge righteous judgment' Cyril reads as Christ's hermeneutical principle for theological discernment. The Jews were judging based on surface considerations (the Sabbath violation appeared); Christ calls them to deeper judgment (the inner meaning of the law as service to humanity). For Cyril this verse is the dominical warrant for the typological-spiritual exegesis of the Old Testament: the appearance of the text (the literal-historical sense) must be supplemented by the righteous judgment (the spiritual-Christological sense) that recognizes Christ in every passage. This grounds the entire Alexandrian hermeneutical method.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk IV.24 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink' Cyril notes the timing with care: on the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, when the temple's water-libation ceremony reached its climax, Christ stood up to offer Himself as the true reality the ceremony only prefigured. The water libation pleaded for the autumn rains; Christ offers the Living Water of the Spirit that gives eternal life. The 'standing' (statheis) and 'crying' (ekraxen) Cyril takes as proleptic posture of the eschatological Christ — standing as the judge, crying as the herald of salvation. The Tewahedo Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase Anaphora prayers for the Holy Spirit echo this passage's invitation.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk V.37 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: 'He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly (koilias) shall flow rivers of living water' Cyril reads as the pneumatological promise: the Spirit indwelling the believer becomes a perpetual source overflowing to others. The 'rivers' (plural — potamoi) signify both abundance (not merely a trickle) and diversity (different charisms flowing through different believers). The 'belly' (koilias) Cyril interprets as the heart in its biblical-Hebraic sense — the seat of personal life — not the digestive organ. The Tewahedo baptismal liturgy preserves this verse as one of the dominical promises connected to the chrismation that immediately follows baptism: the Spirit poured out becomes the believer's own source of life-giving witness to others.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk V.38 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: John's interpretive aside — 'This spake He of the Spirit, which they that believe on Him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified' — Cyril takes as decisive for the post-Pentecost-character of the Spirit's full gift. 'Was not yet' (oupō ēn) does NOT mean the Spirit did not exist (Cyril rejects this Origenist misreading) but that the Spirit had not yet been GIVEN in the new-covenant fullness — that giving awaits the Cross-Resurrection-Ascension sequence ('glorified' here meaning the entire paschal exaltation, not merely Resurrection appearance). After Pentecost the Spirit indwells the Church permanently as in 7:38; before Pentecost the Spirit comes intermittently as in the Old Testament prophets. This verse anchors Cyril's pneumatology of progressive economy.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk V.39 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

entries.work: Commentary on the Gospel of John
entries.summary: The temple officers' report — 'Never man spake like this Man' (oudepote elalēsen houtōs anthrōpos) — Cyril takes as inspired witness from unwilling sources. The very men sent to arrest Christ become the heralds of His unique authority: they cannot perform their task because the sheer weight of His word disarms them. Cyril notes the linguistic precision: not merely 'never has anyone spoken' but specifically 'never man' (anthrōpos) — implying recognition that more than a mere man speaks here. The verse becomes for Cyril the historical-witness confirmation of the Logos's incarnate authority — even those resistant to faith bear unintended testimony to it.
entries.attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk V.46 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
